comparison: Perfect agreement on RNN modeling claims (C4, C5, C31-C37, C42-C43). Both evaluations find the computational evidence SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights the model's accuracy and mechanistic validation through lesion experiments. Peer review (Reviewer 2) explicitly praises the phasic gain modeling as 'original' and notes it resolves previous concerns about network effects.

Strong disagreement on main conclusions (C1, C24, C62-C63, C66). OpenEval rates these SUPPORTED based on converging evidence from all three methods. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 stating 'the demonstration of the causal role of gain modulation in perceptual switches is partial' and raising fundamental concerns about whether effects relate to 'the perceptual switch itself, to attention, or to the detection of behaviourally relevant events.'

Significant disagreement on pupillometry evidence (C2, C25-C30). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, emphasizing strong statistical evidence (p=2.3×10⁻¹⁹) and temporal correlation. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 questioning specificity ('unclear whether the effects...are related to the perceptual switch itself, to attention, or to the detection of behaviourally relevant events') and noting lack of catch trials to control for expectation effects.

Disagreement on fMRI findings (C6-C7, C45, C50-C53, C58-C61). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, highlighting low-dimensional patterns, significant switch-related activity, and validation of computational predictions. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 raising the same specificity concerns as with pupillometry and noting the work is 'correlative' rather than demonstrating causality.

Agreement on network topology analysis (C56-C57). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on permutation test results (p<0.05). Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with no specific challenges raised and implicit acceptance through editor's positive assessment of 'solid evidence.'

Partial overlap on validation methods (C54-C55). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for neurosynth correlation and partial correlation analyses. Peer review rates the broader fMRI findings UNCERTAIN due to specificity concerns, but does not specifically challenge these particular validation analyses.

Agreement on basic experimental methods (C68-C74, C77-C78). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate controls and adequate sample sizes. Peer review accepts the methodological approach, with Reviewer 3 acknowledging fMRI catch trials, though noting pupil study lacked such controls.

Disagreement on RNN architecture (C75-C76). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, describing the model as 'well-specified with biologically-inspired constraints.' Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 raising concerns that the RNN knows target categories in advance while 'observers in the task don't know in advance the identity of the last image,' suggesting the model may not adequately capture the human task.

Agreement on theoretical background (C8-C23). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate contextualization within established frameworks. Peer review (editor and Reviewer 3) commends the 'highly integrative nature' combining different fields and viewpoints, describing this as 'rare in the field' and 'very useful.'

Agreement on pupil-neuromodulation link (C3). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting C3 establishes theoretical link through citations. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED (C3, C22), with editor describing pupillometry as 'an indirect proxy of neuromodulatory activity' and Reviewer 3 acknowledging it as 'correlative (which is already very informative)' without disputing validity.

Agreement on interpretive conclusions (C64-C65, C67). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting appropriate connection to broader literature though 'somewhat speculative.' Peer review also rates SUPPORTED as part of broader theoretical foundations, with no specific challenges to these interpretive claims.

Agreement on prior work citation (C44). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting it provides important context from same research group. Peer review includes this in broader SUPPORTED evaluation of theoretical foundations without specific challenge.
